title: What changes when a voice agent speaks Spanish -
summary: Moving a voice agent to Spanish can take one setting. Running it safely on regulated collections calls takes native-speaker QA, the customer's approved scripts and a check that Spanish callers get the same options as English callers.
body_markdown:
By Karan Ashta


In 2017, the CFPB found that a major card issuer had withheld certain collection offers from cardholders who asked to be contacted in Spanish. In total, about $95 million went back to roughly 222,000 consumers affected by these and related practices5. Regulators can treat worse outcomes for one language group as a sign of national-origin discrimination, whatever the cause.


Many consumers would rather sort out a debt in their own language, and a voice agent that speaks Spanish lets a collections team reach them without hiring bilingual staff. The same agent also makes the card issuer's mistake easier to repeat, because the models behind it are multilingual out of the box: moving an agent to Spanish can take one setting, and nobody on the engineering or deployment team needs to speak the language. Many vendors now advertise dozens of languages, but few explain how they test each one.


Getting an agent to speak Spanish takes little effort, while running it safely on regulated Spanish calls takes native-speaker QA, the customer's approved scripts, and a check that Spanish callers get the same options as English callers. Our voice agent now takes Spanish calls with all three in place. The examples below come from our own Spanish testing.


## It hears the wrong thing


A public benchmark of mixed Spanish-English speech found errors cluster on case numbers, names and dates3.


Caller said What went wrong Result


"Sí" ("yes") to a payment plan Heard as the English word "see" The agent keeps asking questions instead of taking the payment


"Deseo pagar el total" ("I want to pay the full balance") Heard as "en total" ("in total…") The agent waits for an amount the caller already gave


"El quince" ("on the 15th") Heard as "en quince días" ("in 15 days") The payment is expected on the wrong date, and the account is flagged as a broken promise to pay


"Sesenta" (60) Heard as "setenta" (70) The caller is charged more than they agreed to


Callers also read numbers in pairs, so a card ending 4512 often comes out as "cuarenta y cinco, doce" ("forty-five, twelve"). The fix is the same in every case: the agent reads back each amount and date, and every card or account number digit by digit, before acting on it.


## It switches to English mid-call


The most common issue our Spanish QA lead found was transition lines like "Please hold" and "Thank you for your patience" coming out in English. The outcome of the call didn't change, so reviewers passed it, but a caller who doesn't speak English suddenly heard a sentence they couldn't follow.


A different problem starts with the caller, since many US Spanish speakers use English words like "hold," "balance" or "autopay" inside Spanish sentences.


What the caller says What the agent should do


"¿Por qué hay un hold en mi cuenta?" ("Why is there a hold on my account?") Stay in Spanish. "Hold" is just a word they use


"¿Puede hablar en inglés, por favor?" ("Can you speak English, please?") Switch to English, because the caller asked for it


Our agent originally switched to English on the first line. A rule that keeps the agent in Spanish no matter what fixes that, but then it ignores the second caller, so every language fix is tested against both.


The worst place for a switch is in the middle of a required notice. A caller who only speaks Spanish misses whatever part is said in English, even though every word was read. Regulation F requires these disclosures in the language of the call, and in both languages when a call mixes them1.


## It changes what an approved script means


An approved English script says an account "may be reported" to the credit bureaus. A loose Spanish rendering says it "va a ser reportada" ("will be reported"). One word turns a disclosure into a promised consequence, and the FDCPA prohibits threatening action that isn't intended or can't legally be taken2.


## Automated checks don't catch it


Our Spanish QA lead puts it simply: a transcript can look perfectly acceptable while the call itself had problems. When a caller said "correcto," the transcript recorded the English "correct," and an automated judge read it as a valid confirmation.


Research backs this up: when AI judges scored the same content in 25 languages, their verdicts agreed only fairly from one language to the next4. Native speakers still need to check an AI judge before it scores Spanish calls.


## The record has to be right too


Our AI-native call monitoring application transcribes, translates and checks every call for compliance, whether the agent is AI or human. On a bilingual call, our monitoring identifies the language of each speaker and translates only what was said in Spanish. When a system translates English as if it were Spanish, the record changes:


Agent said Stored as Why


"on a recorded line" "on a remembered line" Spanish "recordado" means "remembered"


"nine" "girl" Spanish "niña" means "girl"


"cents" "hundred" Spanish "cien" means "hundred"


"hundred" "sunk" Spanish "hundido" means "sunk"


The first row is the costly one because the recording notice was given, but the compliance check reports it missing.


## How we do Spanish right


A new language goes live only after it passes the same tests as English, with every required notice taken from the customer's approved scripts.


Step What it does What we test in Spanish


1. Hearing A multilingual speech model that detects the language of every turn, chosen after testing several speech models Hundreds of Spanish test clips: short answers, amounts, dates, card numbers, English words mixed into Spanish


2. Deciding what to say Picks the response and the wording Full simulated calls in Spanish, scored on the same checklist as English


3. Speaking Turns the response into voice How amounts, ZIP codes and English labels sound


4. Retesting every fix Checks that a fix didn't break something else Every native reviewer finding becomes a permanent automated test, and every fix is tested in both directions


5. Same call, both languages Runs identical scenarios in English and Spanish Whether callers are offered the same payment plans, hardship options and transfers


Native reviewers also check that the agent stays formal and answers both questions when a caller asks two at once.


## Before you launch a language


Questions worth asking any voice AI vendor, including us:


- Who on your team speaks the language, and do they review live calls?
- Do required notices come from approved scripts in that language, or from the model's own translation?
- Do you compare offers and outcomes between English and Spanish callers on the same scenarios?
- Has your automated scoring been checked against native speakers in that language?
